title: A comparative study of handling imbalanced data using generative adversarial networks for machine learning based software fault prediction
summary: Compares five GAN variants, CopulaGAN, VanillaGAN, CTGAN, TGAN and WGANGP, as oversampling methods for software fault prediction, pairing each with Recursive Feature Elimination for feature selection and separately with autoencoders for feature extraction, then training six classifiers (Random Forest, XGBoost, HistGradientBoosting, MLP, Extra Trees, AdaBoost) on five PROMISE defect datasets (CM1, KC1, KC2, PC1, JM1) and scoring precision, recall, F1, AUC and MCC, with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test against SMOTE, Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN and random undersampling. The conclusion is that the GAN oversamplers beat the interpolation-based baselines and that CTGAN is the best performer, followed by WGANGP and VanillaGAN, with the RFE plus CTGAN and autoencoder plus CTGAN pairings strongest across datasets. The paper is in the index because two of the five generators it runs are SDV synthesizers and it says so outright: CopulaGAN is described as a variation of CTGAN presented in the SDV open source library, with the SDV documentation page for the CopulaGAN synthesizer given as the reference, and its data preparation is attributed to Reversible Data Transformation. The CTGAN and CopulaGAN hyperparameter tables list embedding dim, generator dim, discriminator dim, generator lr, generator decay, discriminator lr and discriminator decay at their package defaults, which are the CTGANSynthesizer constructor arguments, so the sdv-dev package was run rather than an independent reimplementation. TGAN is credited to Xu and Veeramachaneni's earlier tabular GAN, and CTGAN's mode-specific normalization by variational Gaussian mixture and its conditional generator with training-by-sampling are reproduced in the method section.

title: Towards hybrid over- and under-sampling combination methods for class imbalanced datasets: an experimental study
summary: An experimental study of which ORDER to combine under-sampling and over-sampling for class imbalanced data, run over 44 KEEL benchmark datasets with three over-sampling algorithms (SMOTE, CTGAN and TGAN) and three instance-selection algorithms (IB3, DROP3 and GA), scored by AUC under C4.5 and random forest classifiers. The headline finding is that instance selection carries most of the benefit: with IB3 chosen as the under-sampler, adding an over-sampling step brings no significant further improvement, and where both steps are required on large or extremely imbalanced data, instance selection first and over-sampling second is the better order. The paper is in the index because CTGAN is one of the three over-sampling algorithms actually executed rather than merely cited: section 4.4.2 and table 6 report random forest AUC for CTGAN alone, for CTGAN followed by IB3 and for IB3 followed by CTGAN, with the last of these tying for the highest rate reported anywhere in the paper, and the authors conclude that performing IB3 first is a stable procedure that makes different over-sampling methods produce similar results. CTGAN and TGAN are introduced as the tabular GAN variants proposed to generate discrete and continuous variables simultaneously, so the entry records both as generators the paper runs inside a comparison whose subject is the combination order rather than the generators themselves.
evidence: section 1 states that the performance of three over-sampling methods is considered, including SMOTE and two Generative Adversarial Network variants, Tabular GAN (TGAN) and Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN), citing Xu et al. 2019 for CTGAN; section 4.1.2 states that GAN can only handle unstructured data such as images and text and that to deal with structured data TGAN and CTGAN were proposed to simultaneously generate discrete and continuous variables; section 4.4.2 states that the authors further compare SMOTE with CTGAN and GAN for the over-sampling task to examine the effect on instance selection by IB3, that the performance of CTGAN and TGAN in combination with IB3 is very similar, and that the best result is obtained by performing instance selection first and over-sampling second; table 6 reports random forest AUC of 0.809 for CTGAN alone, 0.800 for CTGAN plus IB3 and 0.864 for IB3 plus CTGAN, against 0.858 for IB3 alone and 0.827 for SMOTE; the conclusion states that the results obtained using other over-sampling methods such as TGAN and CTGAN are similar. Two naming defects are recorded as the paper has them rather than corrected: TGAN is cited in section 1 and section 4.1.2 to Goodfellow et al. 2014 instead of to Xu and Veeramachaneni, and the TGAN columns of table 6 are headed VGAN.

title: Investigating landslide data balancing for susceptibility mapping using generative and machine learning models
summary: Studies how to balance a landslide inventory for susceptibility mapping in Lianghe County, Yunnan, where mapped landslides (positive samples) are far scarcer and non-landslide cells (negative samples) far less reliable than a classifier needs. Two problems are attacked at once: negative samples are screened with a self-training semi-supervised SVM, and positive samples are augmented with CTGAN, a plain GAN and SMOTE in increments of 50 to 250 synthetic records. Three classifiers, a 1D CNN-LSTM, a random forest and a gradient boosted decision tree, are trained on ten environmental factors and scored by AUC and F1. Screening the negatives alone lifts AUC from 0.778, 0.869 and 0.849 to 0.837, 0.936 and 0.877, and the best model in the study is a random forest trained with 200 CTGAN-generated positive samples at AUC 0.962. A t-SNE comparison of real against synthetic points is used to argue that SMOTE output sits tightly around the real data while CTGAN output fills the distributional space, giving more diversity while still simulating the overall distribution. The paper is in the index because CTGAN is the generator behind its best result: it is credited to Xu et al. 2019, its conditional generator with training-by-sampling and its Gaussian-mixture normalization of continuous columns are reproduced in the method section as the reason it suits landslide data mixing continuous factors such as elevation and slope with discrete ones such as lithology and land use, and its synthetic samples are what the winning random forest is trained on. No library is named anywhere in the text, so the entry keys to the ctgan component on the strength of the method description and the runs reported.
evidence: the abstract states that the paper researches the effectiveness of three oversampling models in generating positive samples for landslides, Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Networks (CTGAN), Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and the traditional SMOTE algorithm, and that the RF model augmented with 200 positive samples generated by CTGAN achieves the highest prediction accuracy in the study at AUC 0.962; the introduction states that CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) is a novel generative model that addresses the imbalance of tabular data through conditional generators and training-by-sampling and is more suitable for handling landslide data containing both continuous and discrete data than traditional GAN methods; the CTGAN section states that it synthesizes data by fitting conditional probability distributions of discrete data columns and normalizing them with a Gaussian mixture model, that it trains using the PacGAN framework and WGAN loss with gradient penalty, and reproduces the conditional generator equations; the discussion states that the highest accuracy is achieved after 200 positive samples are augmented by CTGAN and predicted by RF model training, and that the generated data of CTGAN does not all surround the real data but instead fills up the distributional space of the real data, indicating diversity while effectively simulating the overall distribution. No implementation library is named at any point.

title: A conditional input-based GAN for generating spatio-temporal motor imagery electroencephalograph data
summary: Proposes a conditional-input temporal GAN for augmenting motor imagery EEG, combining adversarial training with a supervised autoregressive loss and an embedding and recovery autoencoder so that spatio-temporal structure survives generation, with class labels fed to both generator and discriminator through an extra input layer, and all four components built from three-layer GRU networks. Sample quality is assessed by an inverted Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, KL divergence, SVC and logistic detection scores and a train-on-synthetic test-on-real predictive score, plus PCA and t-SNE views, and a 1D temporal CNN trained purely on synthetic EEG reaches 94.1 percent accuracy on real test data against 85 percent without augmentation. The paper is in the index because its entire comparison set is SDV: it benchmarks the proposed model against CTGAN, TVAE and CopulaGAN and reports numbers for all three, and its discussion argues that CTGAN does not take the time factor into account, which is the gap the proposed architecture is built to close. CTGAN and TVAE are cited to Xu et al. 2019, and CopulaGAN ships only in SDV, so the trio identifies the SDV tabular API as the baseline suite even though the library itself is never named.
evidence: section 1.3 states that the authors analyze three data augmentation models, Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN), Tabular Variational Auto-encoders (TVAE) and Copula GAN, due to their widespread application in augmentation and ease of implementation, and assess their impact on the performance of various machine learning and deep learning models; section 4.3 states that the quality of the generated sample is evaluated by comparing it with other state-of-the-art models, Copula GAN, Conditional Tabular GAN and Tabular Variational Auto-encoders; table 5 reports the inverted KS test and KL divergence as 0.8996 and 0.799 for CTGAN, 0.9171 and 0.800 for Copula GAN and 0.9530 and 0.916 for TVAE against 0.8940 and 0.7674 for the proposed model, with SVC detection, logistic detection and predictive score for each; figure 4 plots a cumulative distribution graph per model; section 5 states that EEG data is recorded across time but CTGAN does not take into consideration the time factor, and that in order to capture the temporal dynamics adversarial learning has been combined together with autoregressive models, and separately that Copula GAN suffers from a permutation invariance problem and that TVAE must remember all the temporal dynamics of data in latent space. CTGAN and TVAE are both keyed to the Xu et al. 2019 conditional GAN reference; Copula GAN is keyed instead to a 2021 MTCopula synthetic complex data generation paper, which is recorded as the paper has it rather than corrected.
